title: Seven-Repo Data Intelligence Audit
subtitle: Seven repositories were graded on the same seven-part rubric — collecting data, scoring it, linking it, finding insights, writing outputs at different lengths, choosing which model runs, and working inside Claude Code and Codex — to see how they could combine into one research workflow.

dimensions.label: Data collection
dimensions.question: sources it can ingest (web search, scraping, APIs, files, PDFs, DBs), how (scheduled? on-demand?), formats.

dimensions.label: Assessment & categorization
dimensions.question: scoring, classification, tagging, credibility/tier grading, dedup, taxonomy.

dimensions.label: Graphs & structures
dimensions.question: knowledge graph, entity/relationship extraction, linking, clustering, timelines, hierarchies; storage (DB, JSON, graph DB); visualization.

dimensions.label: Insight extraction
dimensions.question: trend detection, comparison, contradiction detection, gap analysis, “so-what” generation.

dimensions.label: Synthesis at multiple lengths
dimensions.question: long report, short report, key highlights/bullets, PowerPoint outline + slide text, other (email, memo, exec summary). Name the exact templates/prompts/renderers.

dimensions.label: Model flexibility
dimensions.question: which providers, is there a provider abstraction (single interface / factory / router), local (Ollama, MLX, llama.cpp, LM Studio) vs cloud (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, ...), embeddings model choice, config surface (env vars, config file), fallback/routing logic.

dimensions.label: Codex + Claude Code integration
dimensions.question: is it a Claude Code plugin (skills/commands/agents/hooks/MCP)? Codex (AGENTS.md, codex exec)? Both? Or standalone app/API? How does an agent invoke it?

stages.label: Collect data
stages.optimal: The collector agent should own this stage. Make Omniparse the single front door for files — the research plugin already bundles it and it reads Excel, PowerPoint (PPTX), PDF and Python files in one pass — and add stratagem's SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) filing search plus local-smartz's page scraper and web search for the sources Omniparse cannot reach. Three repos tie at the top here, since stratagem, market-research and market-research-platform all read widely, and stratagem wins because it brings the one source nobody else has.

stages.label: Assess and score
stages.optimal: The assessor agent should own this stage and reuse the research plugin's scoring exactly as it stands: it sorts source domains into four trust tiers, blocks known misinformation sites, checks claims four ways, and writes one confidence mark back onto each entry. Fold the market research platform's list of roughly 55 rated domains into that seed list, and add its five-point quality rubric and stratagem's report critic so finished outputs get graded too. Nothing else here is close — the research plugin is the only repo rated mature on this.

stages.label: Link and structure
stages.optimal: The linker agent should own this stage, starting from the research plugin's store, which already turns wiki-style links into two-way backlinks and rebuilds topic and tag hub pages, with the market research platform's vector store bolted on so entries can be found by meaning rather than keyword alone. Then write the missing half: tables for the people, companies and products an entry mentions, and the relationships between them. This is the only stage where no repo has a working answer, so most of the work here is new.

stages.label: Find insights
stages.optimal: The analyst agent should own this stage. Take local-smartz's fact-check loop, which names the facts a draft is missing and sends the researcher back for them up to twice, and pair it with stratagem's claim grading and its compare-multiple-periods financial prompts. The two tie on score, and local-smartz wins because its loop runs in code rather than living only in a prompt; on top of both, add a pass that compares stored facts across entries so the prompts narrate findings instead of discovering them.

stages.label: Write outputs (long, short, highlights, slides)
stages.optimal: The writer agent should own this stage, combining stratagem's four renderers — Markdown, PowerPoint (PPTX), Word (DOCX) and web page — with the market research platform's email, meeting-notes and outline writers into one package. Those two tie at the top, and stratagem leads because it is the only repo that writes a real PowerPoint file instead of a slide outline in text. The agent takes a length and picks the matching template.

stages.label: Run models (local or cloud)
stages.optimal: The model-runner should own this stage and use local-smartz's router: one interface over Ollama on your machine plus Anthropic, OpenAI and Groq in the cloud, with a privacy switch that refuses cloud calls when its own settings cannot be read. Graft the market research platform's Apple-silicon local runner (MLX) in as a fifth option. local-smartz ties with market-research here and wins because its router is Python, fails safe, and pins a model per role.

stages.label: Work inside Claude Code / Codex
stages.optimal: The coordinator should own this stage and ship inside the research plugin's existing packaging — it is the only tool here installed in both Claude Code and Codex, with 22 commands, a skill, and a hook that re-reads files as you save them. Each stage agent becomes another skill beside those commands, so nothing new has to be installed. Later, a small tool server following the pattern stratagem already uses would let local-smartz reach the same tools, and its plugin support could then be switched on by default.

subjects.name: market-intel
subjects.kindNote: Abandoned Next.js prototype; nothing behind the screens
subjects.oneLiner: An abandoned web prototype for a feed-to-news-brief product. Every screen is drawn from sample data typed into the source, and the backend those screens were meant to call was deleted and never replaced.

plain.whatItDoes: It shows what a news-brief product would look like: a source list, a grid of articles, and a summary panel. None of it is real — the articles, the categories and the summaries are all fixed text in the source, and every button waits a second or two to imitate work before showing the same values back. No network request is ever made.
plain.howUsed: Nothing uses it. Its git history is broken, all 40 of its tests fail before they run, and it has not been touched since June 2025.
plain.unique: Its one asset is a test that fully records the contract of the summarising endpoint someone deleted.

health.summary: Dead — .git/refs missing, 40/40 tests fail at import, all data mocked

pipeline.overview: Nothing moves. The screens are drawn from fixed sample data typed into the source, and each button waits a second or two to imitate work before showing the same values back.

effectiveness.why: The backend was deleted and never replaced, so no data enters or leaves the app and all 40 tests fail before they run.

flow.how: It does not do this.
flow.why: There is no fetcher, feed reader or schedule, and the addresses its data code calls do not exist.

flow.how: It filters sample articles against a hand-typed list of twelve categories.
flow.why: Filtering is not scoring — nothing rates, tags or de-duplicates anything.

flow.how: It does not do this.
flow.why: There is no linking, clustering or storage; the only database artifact is two permission rules with no tables.

flow.how: It does not do this.
flow.why: The “why it matters” and “bottom line” lines are typed into the sample data by hand.

flow.how: It pastes fixed fields into one markdown layout after a two-second pause.
flow.why: One length, no model, and the only real specification survives in a test.

flow.how: It does not do this.
flow.why: The OpenAI package is declared and imported by nothing outside test doubles.

flow.how: It carries a list of shell commands Claude Code is allowed to run, and nothing else.
flow.why: An agent can only treat it as an ordinary folder of code; nothing in it is callable.

D1.evidence: No fetcher, no RSS parser, no scheduler, no rss-parser/cheerio dep. components/rss-controls.tsx:28-46 "Add source" is setTimeout(1000) + local useState; feed list is mockSources at :35-39. lib/database-api.ts:7,25,38,57,70,88 fetches /api/rss-sources, /api/articles, /api/summaries — none of those routes exist (app/ contains only layout.tsx, page.tsx, test/page.tsx), and DatabaseAPI has zero importers.
D1.cite: components/rss-controls.tsx:28-46; :35-39; lib/database-api.ts:7,25,38,57,70,88; /api/rss-sources; /api/articles; /api/summaries; app/; layout.tsx; page.tsx; test/page.tsx
D1.plain: Nothing in it fetches anything. The “add source” button waits one second and then stores the name in the page's own memory, and the code that would call a backend points at web addresses that do not exist.

D2.evidence: Category taxonomy is a 12-string literal array app/page.tsx:70-74; filtering is article.categories.some(...) app/page.tsx:97-101. No scoring, credibility tiering, dedup, or auto-tagging anywhere.
D2.plain: Categories are a hand-typed list of twelve words, used only to filter the fake articles on screen. There is no scoring, no trust rating, and no duplicate removal.

D3.evidence: No graph/vector/entity code. supabase-fix.sql:3-12 is the only persistence artifact — two RLS policies on an articles table; no schema, no migrations, no Supabase client instantiated despite @supabase/supabase-js in package.json:52.
D3.plain: Nothing links, clusters or stores anything. The only trace of a database is two permission rules in a leftover SQL file, with no tables and no connection ever opened.

D4.evidence: whyItMatters / keyDetails / bottomLine are literal strings in the mock fixtures (app/page.tsx:18-24, components/news-grid.tsx:14-21), rendered verbatim by components/news-card.tsx:76-107. No trend, comparison, contradiction, or gap logic.
D4.plain: The “why it matters” and “bottom line” lines are typed into the fake data by hand and printed straight back out. No comparison, trend or gap logic exists.

D5.evidence: One length only, and it is string interpolation, not generation: components/summary-panel.tsx:24-41 setTimeout(2000) then template-literals the fixture fields into a "Why it matters / Key insights / Bottom line / Sources" markdown block. The real renderer's contract survives only as a test expectation — __tests__/api/summarize.test.ts:49-55 asserts a 3-part "Key Takeaway / Why it matters / Bulleted highlights" format from gpt-4o, temperature: 0, max_tokens: 500, system prompt containing "You are an expert summary assistant". No docx/pptx/email/exec-summary.
D5.plain: One length only, and it is not written by a model: the panel waits two seconds and pastes the fake fields into a fixed layout. The real summariser was deleted, and only its test survives — recording exactly the model, the settings and the output shape it used to produce.

D6.evidence: openai@^5.3.0 is declared (package.json:60) and imported by nothing outside test mocks. Sole grep hits in shipping code are the words "OpenAI"/"GPT-5" inside mock headlines (components/news-grid.tsx:8-9). No provider abstraction, no local runtime, no embeddings, no router/fallback. Config surface = 3 keys in .env.local (NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY), all unread by source.
D6.plain: The OpenAI package is listed as a dependency and imported by nothing outside test doubles. Three keys sit in the environment file, and no code reads any of them.

D7.evidence: .claude/settings.local.json is a 34-entry Bash permission allowlist only — no skills, commands, agents, hooks, MCP, plugin.json, or AGENTS.md. .navgator/architecture/ holds a NavGator scan (181 nodes / 361 edges, metrics.json:4-7, generated 2026-07-12). An agent can only drive it as a plain repo; nothing is callable.
D7.plain: It carries a list of 34 shell commands Claude Code is allowed to run, and nothing else — no commands, skills, agents or tool server. An agent can only treat it as an ordinary folder of code.

strengths: The deleted summariser's contract is fully recoverable from its test: the exact model, the settings, the opening system prompt, the output shape and every error branch.
The news card is a genuinely reusable structured-brief component — a lead that expands into why it matters, key details, bottom line and sources — and it maps cleanly onto any summary.
Its integration test only runs when an API key is present, which is the right way to gate live calls in a shared suite.
A preflight script and a written post-mortem capture a real Next.js failure — a dev server that reports ready but serves a blank page — that transfers to sibling apps.
gaps: The backend is missing, not stubbed. Removing a folder that was shadowing the app router took the summarising endpoint with it, stranding all 40 tests and all six data methods. The interface never makes a network request.
Every so-called AI behaviour is a timer faking delay: refresh, add source, summarise and save each wait a second or two and then show fixed data.
Git is broken. The references folder is missing, so about two weeks of edits have no recoverable history and git commands are unusable until it is rebuilt from the log.
An environment file holds a live-looking OpenAI key plus Supabase credentials, protected only by the ignore rules, and no code reads any of the three.

reuse.what: The executable specification for a summary endpoint — model, settings, system prompt, response shape and error branches. Port it as the contract test for the combined repo's summariser; it is worth more than the code it tested.
A self-contained structured-brief card: a collapsed lead that expands into why it matters, key details, bottom line and source links. Drop it in for any summary with those fields.
The markdown layout — why it matters, key insights, bottom line, sources — reusable as the specification for what a model should output, minus the fake delay.
A complete, current component set already reconciled with the latest React and Tailwind; cheaper to copy than to rebuild.
Preflight and repair scripts for a Next.js dev server, useful in any sibling Next.js app.

subjects.role: Retire it. Salvage the summariser's contract test and the news card; the feed-reading job moves to the new scheduled collector.

subjects.name: market-research
subjects.kindNote: Web app + `mra` command line + Mac shell
subjects.oneLiner: A local-first, privacy-tiered document research app — a browser interface, an `mra` command line and a thin Mac shell — that reads files and web pages, indexes them locally for keyword and meaning-based search, and writes a cited, conclusion-first summary using Ollama or a cloud model.

plain.whatItDoes: You give it files or web addresses and it reads them, splits the text into chunks, and indexes them on your machine so it can find the right passages by keyword and by meaning. It then clusters the best passages by theme, merges them in two passes, and returns a conclusion with three to five supporting arguments and cited evidence. Anything that looks confidential is kept away from the cloud parser.
plain.howUsed: You open the browser interface, run the `mra` command line, or use the Mac shell. There is no plugin, so an agent calls the command line or the local web routes.
plain.unique: It is the only tool here that reranks its search results with a small model running in the same process.

pipeline.overview: You hand it files or web addresses, it extracts the text, splits it into chunks, and indexes them locally for keyword and meaning-based search. A two-pass summariser then clusters the best chunks by theme, merges them, and returns a conclusion-first summary with citations, either in the browser or from the command line.

effectiveness.why: The read, index and summarise path genuinely works offline end to end, but it produces one shape of answer and the browser interface cannot export it.

flow.how: It reads PDF, Excel, CSV, PowerPoint (PPTX) and Word (DOCX) files and scrapes pages, sending sensitive documents to a local parser instead of a cloud one.
flow.why: Broad format coverage and a real privacy rule, but only when you ask — nothing is scheduled.

flow.how: It scores each parse for confidence, tags themes, and drops near-duplicates within a run.
flow.why: Useful signals about the parse, but no judgement about the source.

flow.how: It groups chunks by theme and stores them in a local vector database, with citations pointing back to chunk numbers.
flow.why: Grouping is not linking — nothing connects the same company or product across documents.

flow.how: It asks the model, in one line of prompt, to point out where excerpts disagree.
flow.why: An instruction, not a detector.

flow.how: It writes a conclusion with three to five supporting arguments and cited evidence, exportable as Word (DOCX) or JSON from the command line.
flow.why: Strong single shape, but no short, highlight or slide variants, and no export from the browser.

flow.how: It routes between Ollama on your machine, OpenAI and Groq after a health check, and can be forced local-only.
flow.why: Real choice with per-model prices and fallbacks, plus a reranker running in the same process.

flow.how: An agent runs its `mra` command line or calls the local web routes.
flow.why: Clean entry points, but nothing registers with Claude Code or Codex.

D1.evidence: src/lib/parsers/fileRouter.ts:104-162 routes PDF/XLSX/CSV/PPTX/DOCX to dedicated parsers; src/lib/parsers/urlScraper.ts:111 scrapes URLs via @tyroneross/scraper-app through api/local/scrape.ts; src/lib/parsers/hybridParser.ts:70-116 picks LlamaParse-cloud vs local per sensitivity; cli/index.ts:144 mra ingest <pathOrUrl>. On-demand only — no scheduler, no web-search, no DB/API connectors.
D1.plain: It reads PDF, Excel, CSV, PowerPoint (PPTX) and Word (DOCX) files and scrapes web pages, choosing a cloud parser or a local one based on how sensitive the document looks. It only runs when you ask it to — there is no schedule and no web search.

D2.evidence: Per-parse confidenceScore (src/lib/parsers/pdf.ts:104, wordParser.ts:115); sensitivity classification by keyword list (hybridParser.ts:315-317 confidential|proprietary|classified) gates cloud vs local; theme tagging (src/lib/utils/themeExtractor.ts:9); naive Jaccard-ish dedup (src/lib/aggregation/aggregationEngine.ts:53-72). No source credibility tiers, no taxonomy, no cross-source dedup.
D2.plain: Every parse gets a confidence number, documents are tagged by theme, and anything that looks confidential is kept away from cloud parsing. It does not rate how trustworthy a source is, and it only removes near-duplicates within a single run.

D3.evidence: No knowledge graph, no entity/relation extraction, no timelines. Only flat theme clustering (src/lib/aggregation/hierarchicalMerge.ts:78 clusterByTheme, with per-source fallback at :95-112) plus storage in LanceDB (src/lib/services/lanceVectorStore.ts:75) and Dexie/IndexedDB (src/lib/db/schema.ts). Citations are chunk-id links, not a graph.
D3.plain: It groups chunks by theme, stores them in a local vector database, and points citations back at chunk numbers. No people, companies or relationships are extracted, and there is no timeline or map of how anything connects.

D4.evidence: Contradiction handling exists only as a prompt instruction (hierarchicalMerge.ts:169 "If the excerpts contradict each other, surface the contradiction…"; same in hierarchicalChunkingService.ts:349). No trend detection, gap analysis, or comparison module — getCostComparison hits are about $ cost, not content (aiService.ts:983).
D4.plain: Contradiction handling is one line of instruction in a prompt asking the model to point out disagreements. Nothing detects trends, compares sources or names what is missing.

D5.evidence: One shape only: PyramidSummary = conclusion → 3-5 arguments → cited evidence (src/lib/constants.ts:184-205 prompts; hierarchicalMerge.ts:335 aggregateHierarchically two-pass cluster-then-merge with chunk re-injection and alias-mapped citations). Renderers: DOCX + JSON in cli/index.ts:332-390 (docx lib), React/markdown in src/components/PyramidSummary/PyramidSummary.tsx:101. No PPTX, no short/long variants, no email/memo. UI "Export Summary" button is dead — onExportSummary is never passed from src/App.tsx (SummaryPanel.tsx:929 renders it permanently disabled).
D5.plain: It produces exactly one shape of answer — a conclusion, three to five supporting arguments, and cited evidence — and can save it as Word (DOCX) or JSON from the command line. The browser app's export button is permanently greyed out because it was never wired up.

D6.evidence: Provider registry src/lib/constants.ts:31-180 (ollama / openai / groq with ~9 Groq models, per-model pricing). Local: src/lib/services/ollamaService.ts:112 (chat + embed, env-overridable VITE_OLLAMA_CHAT_MODEL/_EMBED_MODEL, 404→qwen3:8b-q4_K_M fallback at :219). Router with health probe: aggregationEngine.ts:330 resolveProvider (ollama|openai|auto, localOnly forces local). Local embeddings + local cross-encoder rerank Xenova/bge-reranker-base (src/lib/services/reranker.ts:76). Config surface: .env.example, cli/config.ts (~/.market-research-app/config.json), Settings UI, ModelMigration for retired model IDs. No Anthropic/Gemini/LM Studio.
D6.cite: src/lib/constants.ts:31-180; src/lib/services/ollamaService.ts:112; qwen3:8b-q4_K_M; aggregationEngine.ts:330; Xenova/bge-reranker-base; src/lib/services/reranker.ts:76; .env.example; cli/config.ts; ~/.market-research-app/config.json
D6.plain: It can run entirely on your machine through Ollama or call OpenAI or Groq, with roughly nine Groq models priced in a table, a health check before it chooses, and a local-only switch that forces everything offline. It also reranks results with a small model running in the same process.

D7.evidence: No plugin.json, no .claude-plugin/, no AGENTS.md, no MCP server (searched repo-wide). .claude/agents/*.md holds 8 generic project subagents (backend-api-engineer, system-architect, …) and market-research-app/.claude/settings.json only wires @tyroneross/bookmark snapshot hooks. Agent access is via the mra CLI (cli/bin.ts, commands scrape/parse/ingest/search/summarize/health/config) or the local HTTP routes under api/local/.
D7.plain: There is no plugin packaging and no tool server of any kind. An agent reaches it by running the `mra` command line or calling the local web routes.

strengths: The retrieval stack is genuinely mature: keyword and meaning-based search fused together, a graceful fallback when keyword search is unavailable, a reranker on by default, and an honest note that query rewriting did not help.

The merge step is defensive in ways that read as hard-won — short citation labels so small local models cite correctly, a character budget per cluster, and a per-source fallback documented against a real PowerPoint (PPTX) truncation failure.
A true local-only path runs end to end: read, embed, index, summarise and save a Word (DOCX) file with no cloud calls at all.
Privacy tiering is enforced in code rather than policy — documents that look confidential never reach the cloud parser.
gaps: Roughly 900 lines across three modules have no callers outside themselves.
One so-called local model is really a keyword and pattern matcher with a hardcoded business-term list, now superseded by the Ollama path.

The browser app's export button does nothing, and Word (DOCX) export exists only on the command line. The two summarising paths have also drifted apart — the OpenAI branch still uses the older single-pass prompt with no context re-injection.

Repository hygiene is poor: about 25 status reports at the root, log files, 1.2 MB of committed performance output, screenshots, six ad-hoc test scripts, and a stale duplicate source folder sitting outside the repository.
An environment file sits on disk in the app root — inspect it before sharing the repository.

reuse.what: A local vector store with keyword and meaning-based search fused together, keyword index creation, and a fallback when keyword search is missing; you can swap in your own embedder.
A provider-agnostic cluster-then-merge summariser that returns a conclusion-first summary carrying its citations — the most portable piece here.
A local chat and embedding client with a fallback when the model is missing and a health check, plus a reranker that runs in the same process.
Multi-format extraction with a confidence score per parse and routing that keeps sensitive documents off the cloud parser.
The `mra` command set — scrape, parse, ingest, search, summarise, health — is the cleanest way for an agent to call it and the reference wiring for the whole pipeline.

subjects.role: Reference only. Port its reranking and cluster-then-merge ideas into the spine, and park the app itself.

subjects.name: market-research-platform
subjects.kindNote: Web platform: Python API + React front end
subjects.oneLiner: A local-first research platform with a Python web service and a React front end that reads uploaded documents and web pages, indexes them in a single local database for keyword and meaning-based search, and turns the result into a structured brief plus PowerPoint (PPTX), Word (DOCX), email, notes and outline documents.

plain.whatItDoes: You upload documents or paste web addresses, and it reads them — including scanned pages — chunks the text, and indexes it in one local database that supports both keyword and meaning-based search. It then builds a single structured brief from the retrieved chunks and rates the sources and claims behind it. Five separate writers turn that one brief into finished documents.
plain.howUsed: You use the React front end in a browser, or call the Python web service directly. There is no plugin, so an agent reads a handoff document and calls the web service.
plain.unique: It is the only tool here that reads scanned pages and the only one that writes email, meeting notes and an outline off the same brief.

pipeline.overview: Documents are uploaded or scraped, read in Python, chunked, embedded, and stored in a single local database that serves both keyword and meaning-based search. A map-and-reduce pass turns the retrieved chunks into one structured brief, and five writers turn that brief into finished documents.

effectiveness.why: The path from upload to finished document works and produces the widest range of outputs here, but the knowledge-graph half never runs and its test suite was not executed for this audit.

flow.how: It takes uploads and reads PDF, Word (DOCX), Excel, PowerPoint (PPTX) and scanned images, and fetches pages through a small Node helper.
flow.why: The widest reading list here, scans included, but it only runs when asked.

flow.how: It rates source domains into four trust tiers, checks whether each claim is supported, and grades the finished brief on five dimensions.
flow.why: Deterministic and reusable, and it needs no model to run.

flow.how: It embeds chunks into a local vector store, but the entity graph it defines never runs.
flow.why: No live code path reaches the graph, so the store stays empty and no relationship is ever written.

flow.how: It pulls themes, claims, numbers, risks and actions out of the text with the surrounding context re-attached.
flow.why: Extraction only — the comparison and trend prompts sit in the dead graph code.

flow.how: One brief feeds five writers: PowerPoint (PPTX), Word (DOCX), email, meeting notes and outline.
flow.why: The broadest set of finished documents here, all driven from a single structure.

flow.how: One interface covers Ollama, Apple-silicon local models (MLX) and Claude, with cloud calls blocked unless you allow them.
flow.why: Solid design, but the Apple-silicon path is only half connected and can be sent the wrong model name.

flow.how: An agent calls its web service after reading a handoff document written in prose.
flow.why: No plugin, no commands and no tool server.

D1.evidence: Uploads + in-process parsers for PDF/DOCX/XLSX/PPTX/image-OCR/python (backend/app/parsers/__init__.py); URL ingest scrapes via Node sidecar /scrape (backend/app/api/documents.py:248-330, services/parser-sidecar/src/index.ts). All on-demand — no scheduler, no web-search API anywhere.
D1.plain: It accepts uploads and reads PDF, Word (DOCX), Excel, PowerPoint (PPTX) and scanned images, and fetches web pages through a small Node helper. Everything runs on request: nothing is scheduled and it cannot search the web.

D2.evidence: T1–T4 source-tier scorer with ~55 seeded domains (backend/app/verification/source_scoring.py:15-80); deterministic claim verification + confidence roll-up (backend/app/verification/brief.py:31-60); 5-dimension brief-fidelity rubric (backend/app/reporting/quality.py:1-40). No dedup, no taxonomy/tagging.
D2.plain: It rates source domains into four trust tiers using about 55 known sites, checks whether each claim in a brief is actually supported, and grades the finished brief on five dimensions. It does not remove duplicates or apply a tag taxonomy.

D3.evidence: Graph code exists but the runtime graph is empty. graph_store is imported only by graph/ingestion.py and graph/research.py; both are reachable only through graph/pipeline.py, whose ingestion and research entry points have no callers. The live api/documents.py path never touches graph_store, Kuzu, spaCy, or entity extraction. add_relation also has zero callers, so no relations can be written.
D3.plain: The code for a knowledge graph exists, but nothing in the running app ever calls it, so the graph stays empty. The function that would write a relationship between two things has no callers at all.

D4.evidence: Theme/claim/financial/risk/action extraction with context re-injection (backend/app/reporting/strategy.py:1-20); SWOT/competitive/trend prompts exist in backend/app/graph/research.py:61-66 but that graph is dead (no caller — see D8) and the API says so (backend/app/api/research.py:29-32). No contradiction or gap detection.
D4.plain: It pulls themes, claims, numbers, risks and actions out of documents and feeds the surrounding text back in for context. The comparison and trend prompts sit in the dead graph code, and the live interface says so itself.

D5.evidence: Five renderers off one StrategyBrief: pptx_generator.py:117 (via vendored engines/pptx-builder build_deck + QA gauntlet), docx_generator.py:260, email_generator.py:22, notes_generator.py:23, outline_generator.py:20; registry at backend/app/graph/reporting.py:34-42. Plus Minto-pyramid answer synthesis in /ask (backend/app/api/documents.py:665) and an earnings_call prompt template (backend/app/reporting/prompts/earnings_call.py).

subjects.oneLiner: A multi-agent research app that breaks a question into parts, hands them to twelve specialists that read documents, scrape pages and pull company filings, then renders the result as Markdown, PowerPoint (PPTX), Word (DOCX) or a web page. It ships as a command line, a local web interface and a Mac app, and no longer as a plugin.

plain.whatItDoes: You give it a research question and it plans the work, then runs twelve specialist agents that read documents, scrape web pages and download company filings from the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission). A synthesiser and a critic turn their findings into structured sections. Those sections render straight into finished files, including real PowerPoint decks and spreadsheets.
plain.howUsed: You run its command line with a question, or open its local web interface or Mac app. Its plugin packaging was deleted, so nothing installs into Claude Code or Codex any more.
plain.unique: It is the only repo here that writes a real PowerPoint (PPTX) file and the only one that searches and downloads SEC filings.

pipeline.overview: A question is broken into parts and handed to twelve specialist agents that read documents, scrape pages and pull company filings, each writing findings to files the next agent picks up. A synthesiser and a critic turn those findings into structured sections, which one writer set renders as Markdown, PowerPoint (PPTX), Word (DOCX) or a web page. What it learns is saved as observations and fed back into later runs.

recommendation.bottomLine: The research plugin already answers basic questions well and should keep doing exactly that. What you do not have is a data-analysis pipeline for the complex, multi-stage jobs — tracking a company's quarterly earnings, sizing a new market or business opportunity, reading the financial disclosures behind a merger, or working through a personal decision like which town to move to or which school to pick. You already own a module for nearly every stage of that pipeline, built two to five times over in two languages; the one thing nobody has is a way to link people, companies and products across documents, where the best score anywhere is 2 out of 3.
recommendation.spine: A thin coordinator runs focused stage agents; each stage reuses the strongest existing module and the research plugin remains the store for facts and sources.

flow.title: Collect data
flow.source: The collector agent reuses stratagem's SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) and web collectors plus Omniparse file parsing, and borrows stratagem's extractor-specialist shape; the scheduled feed reader is new.
flow.what: A collector agent gathers the filings, pages and files a question needs and writes what it finds into the research plugin's store. A background job runs saved searches and feeds on a schedule, so long-running topics keep updating themselves.
flow.why: Every reader already exists and is tested, and stratagem is the only repo that reaches company filings. Only the schedule is missing — nothing here runs unattended today.

flow.title: Assess and score
flow.source: The assessor agent reuses the research plugin's scoring and claim verification unchanged, plus the market research platform's five-point quality rubric, and borrows stratagem's source-verifier specialist shape.
flow.what: An assessor agent rates how trustworthy each source is, checks the claims behind it, and marks the entry with one confidence level. It grades finished outputs against the same rubric before they leave the pipeline.
flow.why: The research plugin is the only mature scorer here, it runs without a model, and it already writes its verdict back onto the entry.

flow.title: Link and structure
flow.source: The linker agent is new: entity and relationship tables on top of the research plugin's existing store, with the market research platform's vector store bolted on for search by meaning.
flow.what: A linker agent records the people, companies and products each entry mentions and how they relate, matches the same thing across entries, and exports the result as data plus a simple web view.
flow.why: Nothing existing does this. The market research platform defines a graph but never runs it, and the research plugin links notes to each other rather than the things inside them.

flow.title: Find insights
flow.source: The analyst agent reuses local-smartz's fact-check-and-redo loop and stratagem's contradiction and trend prompts, and borrows local-smartz's analyser-then-fact-checker shape; the deterministic comparison over verified facts is new.
flow.what: An analyst agent compares stored facts across entries: the same measure with different values becomes a contradiction to check, a thing with sources but no claims becomes a gap, and a measure with dates becomes a trend. Anything unsupported goes back for another research pass.
flow.why: Both donors work, but they only narrate. A deterministic pass finds the candidates first, so the model explains rather than discovers.

flow.title: Write outputs (long, short, highlights, slides)
flow.source: The writer agent reuses stratagem's Markdown, PowerPoint (PPTX), Word (DOCX) and web-page renderers plus the market research platform's email, notes and outline writers, and borrows stratagem's synthesiser-then-critic shape.
flow.what: A writer agent takes the length you asked for — long report, short report, highlights, or a deck as an outline with slide text — picks the matching template and renders the file. A critic pass grades the draft before it comes back to you.
flow.why: Between them, stratagem and the market research platform already cover every format anyone here produces, including the only real PowerPoint (PPTX) file.

flow.title: Run models (local or cloud)
flow.source: The model-runner reuses local-smartz's provider router with the market research platform's Apple-silicon runner (MLX) added, and keeps local-smartz's per-role model pinning.
flow.what: Unattended runs pin a model to each stage agent, prefer your own machine, and refuse cloud calls when the settings say local only. Inside Claude Code or Codex there is no runner at all — the assistant makes the calls.
flow.why: local-smartz's router is the most complete here and fails safe, and Apple-silicon support costs one more runner rather than a rewrite.

flow.title: Work inside Claude Code / Codex
flow.source: The coordinator ships inside the research plugin's existing Claude Code and Codex packaging — its commands, one skill per stage agent, and the save hook.
flow.what: A thin coordinator decides which stage agents a question needs and runs them in order, each with its own skill and specialty. Simple questions skip the pipeline and stay with the research plugin's existing commands.
flow.why: The packaging already works in both hosts, so the stage agents ship as skills beside commands people already use, with nothing new to install.

references.name: Perplexity Deep Research
references.flow: It runs a loop: search, read the documents it found, reason about what is still missing, refine the plan, and repeat across dozens of searches and hundreds of sources before writing a cited report. Most runs finish in two to four minutes.
references.borrow: Refine the plan as you learn instead of executing a fixed list of sub-questions.

references.name: AlphaSense Deep Research and Smart Summaries
references.flow: It searches a licensed financial corpus (filings, earnings-call transcripts, broker research, expert-call transcripts, and your uploaded documents), reasons over thousands of hits, and writes a report where every line links to the exact snippet in the source document.
references.borrow: Snippet-level citations that jump to the exact sentence in the source, and a source-priority order that puts filings and transcripts first.

references.name: OpenAI Deep Research
references.flow: It clarifies the ask, then plans and issues its own web searches, reads pages and PDFs, shows its reasoning as it decides which claims to verify next, can run code for data work, and returns a structured report with machine-readable citation spans.
references.borrow: Citations as structured objects (character span, title, URL) so downstream renderers and verifiers can check them, plus a code step for any calculation.

references.name: Google Gemini Deep Research
references.flow: It drafts a multi-point research plan the user can edit and approve, then browses the web (and optionally the user's mail and drive), shows its reasoning as it iterates, and delivers a multi-page report that exports to Docs.
references.borrow: A user-editable plan checkpoint before any search budget is spent.
